opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's been a real selection effect, and it's one people don't talk about enough. Over the last five or so years, a lot of the people in academic machine learning who took AGI most seriously, the ones who thought, "This is actually going to happen, and soon," were exactly the people who had the strongest reasons to go to the labs. If you believe the most important technology in history is being built right now, and the frontier is happening at OpenAI or Anthropic or Google DeepMind, staying in a university looks like a strange choice. The compute is there, the data is there, and frankly the money is there too.

So what's left behind in academia is, on average, a group that's more skeptical, or at least more comfortable treating AGI as a distant or somewhat speculative topic. It's not that everyone who stayed is a skeptic. Plenty of people stay for good reasons: they like teaching, they want intellectual freedom, they don't want to work on whatever the product roadmap demands. But the people who stayed are disproportionately the ones less gripped by the idea that transformative AI is imminent.

That has a few knock-on effects. One is that the academic conversation can lag behind what's actually happening. When you're not seeing the internal scaling results, and your lab can't train anything near frontier scale, it's easy to look at the public models, notice their failures, and conclude it's mostly hype. The people who might have pushed back in faculty meetings or at conferences, saying "no, look at the trend lines," have often left.

Another is a bit more subtle. There's a social dynamic where taking AGI seriously starts to look like something you do once you've decided to leave, almost like a signal that you've joined the industry worldview. So people who stay sometimes feel a mild pressure to distance themselves from it, to be the sober academic voice. That's healthy in some ways, since we need skeptics, but it can turn into a reflexive dismissiveness that isn't really grounded in evidence.

I'd say this has been shifting somewhat. As capabilities have gotten harder to ignore, more of my remaining colleagues have updated, sometimes quite dramatically. But I still think if you surveyed academic ML researchers, you'd get a systematically more conservative picture than you'd get from the people who are closest to the frontier, and part of that is just who chose to leave and who chose to stay.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers who took AGI most seriously were especially likely to leave for AI labs, leaving academia disproportionately more skeptical or comfortable viewing AGI as distant.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's been interesting to watch. I think the honest answer is that there's been a selection effect, and it's shaped the culture in a way that people don't always notice.

The people who left for the labs — OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind — were disproportionately the ones who took the idea of AGI seriously. They looked at scaling trends, they believed the stuff might actually work, and so they went to where the compute was. And the people who stayed were, on average, the ones who were more skeptical, or more interested in theory, or in problems that didn't need ten thousand GPUs.

So what you end up with in a lot of academic ML departments is a kind of residual skepticism that's partly a genuine intellectual position and partly, I think, a bit of a coping mechanism. Because if you've decided to stay, it's much more comfortable to believe that the labs are overhyping things, that it's all just curve fitting, that there's some missing ingredient that only careful academic work will find. I don't say that to be dismissive — I had a lot of those feelings myself. When I came back from my sabbatical at Anthropic, I had to confront how much of my own prior skepticism had been motivated reasoning.

The other thing is that the people who left mostly stopped publishing, or at least stopped publishing the interesting stuff. So the academics who remained didn't see the evidence that was moving the needle inside the labs. They saw the demos and the press releases, which are easy to be cynical about, but not the internal evals and the day-to-day experience of watching capabilities go up every few months. That information asymmetry made the skepticism self-reinforcing.

I'd say that's shifted in the last couple of years, though. It's gotten hard to maintain the "it's all hype" position when your students are using these systems to write their code and draft their papers. So now you see a lot of my colleagues sort of quietly updating, but there's still this reluctance to say "AGI" out loud, because for a long time that word was a signal that you weren't a serious person. The word's lost its stigma faster than people's willingness to use it has caught up.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers who took AGI seriously disproportionately left for AI labs, while those who stayed were on average more skeptical, linking that selection effect to greater skepticism in academic ML.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a selection effect that’s easy to miss. If you think AGI is fairly close, and that the frontier labs are where it’s going to happen, you have a strong reason to go work at one. So the people who remain in academia are disproportionately those who are sceptical of that picture, or who want to pursue a different kind of research.

That means the mood in an academic department can stay quite sceptical even while individual researchers are becoming more convinced: some of the people who change their minds leave. You can look around and think, “Well, most of my colleagues still don’t buy this,” without accounting for who’s no longer in the room.

Of course, leaving isn’t a clean measure of someone’s beliefs. People go for the compute, the salary, or the chance to work with particular colleagues. But I think that sorting makes the gap between the academic and industry outlooks look larger, and makes each group’s view feel more like the consensus than it really is.

r001.rationale: The response explains that researchers who think AGI is fairly close and likely to happen at frontier labs have reason to leave for those labs, leaving academia disproportionately skeptical.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a selection effect, where the people who take AGI most seriously are more likely to leave academia to work on it. So if you look around your department and ask, “How seriously do people take this?” you’re looking at a population that’s been selected partly for being less convinced by it.

And that can become self-reinforcing. The colleagues who would have been making the case that these systems might become much more capable are no longer around for those conversations. I wouldn’t say that explains everyone’s views, but it makes it harder to interpret the mood in academia as an independent judgment about where the field is going.

r001.rationale: It says researchers who take AGI most seriously are more likely to leave academia for AI labs, leaving academic colleagues less convinced and making their outlook more skeptical.
